closenessHoursAtHalf.citation: Hours of time together at which closeness reaches half of full closeness; closeness is hours / (hours + this value), so it grows toward full closeness and never reaches it. Source: Hall (2019), How many hours does it take to make a friend?, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(4): about 50 hours of time together makes a casual friend, 90 a friend and more than 200 a close friend (release figures); in the adult-only sample 94, 164 and 219 hours. The game reads the 90-hour friend threshold as the half-closeness point.

closenessKinHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of time together between relatives without contact, 36 months. Roberts and Dunbar (2015), Managing relationship decay, Human Nature 26(4):426-450, inner-layer retention at wave 3: relatives 102 of 145 (70.3%), friends 69 of 142 (48.6%) over 18 months. Exponential equivalent: 1,078 days. Long-run check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37:65-80 (1,007 Dutch adults aged 18-65, 604 re-interviewed seven years later): 48% of discussion partners and helpers still in the network after seven years, a 2,415-day half-life that includes ongoing contact, so it bounds a full seven-year run rather than decay without contact (figures as reported in the Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009).
closenessKinHalfLifeDays.estimatedFrom: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) relative inner-layer retention converted to an exponential half-life (1,078 days); the sample is 25 school leavers in transition and the paper reports no half-life.

spread.citation: Roberts and Dunbar (2015) derived 1,078 days; Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014) 2,415 days with contact included.

closenessOtherHalfLifeDays.citation: Half-life of time together between people who are not relatives without contact, 18 months. Roberts and Dunbar (2015), Managing relationship decay, Human Nature 26(4):426-450, inner-layer retention at wave 3: friends 69 of 142 (48.6%) over 18 months, an exponential equivalent of 526 days. Long-run check: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37:65-80 (1,007 Dutch adults, 604 re-interviewed seven years later): 48% of discussion partners and helpers remained, a 2,415-day half-life that includes contact (figures as reported in the Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009). The game's share of ties still above their opening closeness after seven years is compared with it in a seven-year run.

farKinContactShare.citation: Visits to a relative living elsewhere in the state, as a share of visits to one living in the same county; Pew 2005: 22% of adults with a parent in a different town see or talk to that parent daily, against 56% in the same town (0.39). Research found no US contact-by-distance table. The nearest measured curve is Hank (2007), J Marriage Fam 69(1):157-173 (SHARE 2004, ten countries): the odds of contact less than weekly rather than daily are 7.39 times higher at 25-100 km and 11.22 times higher beyond 100 km than within 25 km, so most of the loss comes at the first step past about 25 km (15.5 miles). Kept until relatives carry a place.
farKinContactShare.estimatedFrom: Pew Research Center (2005), daily contact with a parent by whether the parent lives in the same town (56%) or a different town (22%): 22/56 = 0.39, applied to visits to any relative elsewhere in the state. Pew counts calls with visits and compares towns, not counties; the CTO accepted it until relatives carry a place (October 10, 2026).

extendedKinVisitShare.citation: Visits to one grandparent, grandchild, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew or a child's other parent, as a share of the GSS frequency of a social evening with any relative. GAME ASSUMPTION, low confidence. GSS relatives social evenings pool to about 60 a year against 50.6 for parents on the game's stand-in category counts, a ratio of 1.19 for the whole group of relatives; 0.25 per relative implies about 4.7 relatives seen, a count no source gives.

spread.reason: The GSS asks about relatives as a group; no source gives visits per extended relative.

tieMissingWeightPerHour.citation: Pull toward contacting a person for each hour of time together the tie has lost since the last contact. Chosen in a sweep of a 600-resident generated Stanwood, Washington town (56 days, seed p15-opening-kin), where higher values added little contact and crowded out other acts. Checked in a 10,001-resident Sacramento town over 91 days (seed p10-drives-proof-2026-10-09): adults made 47.4 visits a year to relatives outside their home, about 91 hours against 170 in ATUS 2019 (28 minutes a day, Kannan and Veazie 2022), and visited each parent 2.5 times as often as each sibling against 1.37 in the GSS. One discretionary act per activation caps the total. GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no external value; the repository's own check lands at 91 of 170 hours a year of visits against ATUS 2019 (54% of target), so it stays a value to re-tune against that target.

spread.reason: No source measures how strongly a fading tie pulls a person to make contact.

kinMoveAwayShare.citation: Share of moves out of the county (ACS 2024 B07401, by state and age) that take a person away from their family, rather than to a nearby county or back home. One value cannot reach both PSID 2013 figures (74.8% nearest parent or grown child within 30 miles, 35.5% all of them). In a generated Sacramento town of 3,000 (seed p10-drives-proof-2026-10-09, with later-life re-aging), 0.3 gives 71.1% and 42.4%, and 0.35 gives 67.1% and 37.5%; 0.35 has the smaller combined miss. Tuned to the PSID 2013 distances (Choi, Schoeni and others 2020, Journal of Marriage and Family, PubMed 33033415); the split of out-of-county moves is a game assumption.

spread.reason: No source splits moves out of the county into moves away from family and short or return moves; PSID reports only the resulting distances (74.8% have the nearest parent or grown child within 30 miles, 35.5% all of them).

kinInterbirthYears.citation: Years between a mother's first and second births in generated sibships and families. NCHS National Health Statistics Reports 179 (Martinez and Daniels 2023, NSFG 2015-2019), Table 6, women with a first birth: 29.5% no second birth, 18.7% within 24 months, 17.3% at 25-36, 10.7% at 37-48, 23.9% at 49 or more. The generator works in whole birth years, so the 2.96-year median is carried as 3.
kinInterbirthYears.estimatedFrom: Median first-to-second interval among women with a second birth, interpolated from NHSR 179 Table 6 (35.5 months, 2.96 years), rounded to the 3 whole years the generator needs.

spread.citation: NHSR 179 Table 6: the median falls in the 25 to 36 month bin.

kinFirstBirthAgeSdYears.citation: Spread in years of a mother's age at first birth around the NCHS national mean for that year. NCHS National Vital Statistics Reports 74(1), Births: Final Data for 2023, Table 3 (1,406,183 first births by mother's age): standard deviation 6.1 years pooled (binned estimate; the mean checks to 27.6 against the published 27.5), 5.1 to 6.3 within Asian, American Indian, Black, White and Hispanic mothers.
kinFirstBirthAgeSdYears.estimatedFrom: Standard deviation computed from the 2023 first births by mother's age bins in NVSR 74(1) Table 3.

spread.citation: NVSR 74(1) Table 3, standard deviation within each race and Hispanic-origin group of mothers.

kinPaternalAgeGapYears.citation: Years by which a generated father is older than the mother. Mean age of fathers 30.9 in 2015 (Khandwala et al. 2017, Human Reproduction 32(10):2110) against mean age of mothers 28.5 in 2015 (NCHS NVSR 74(1), Table III), a gap of 2.4; the NSFG first-birth gap is 2.9 (NHSR 179). NCHS has not published a later father mean in the sources read.
kinPaternalAgeGapYears.estimatedFrom: Difference of the 2015 mean ages of fathers (Khandwala et al. 2017) and mothers (NVSR 74(1) Table III).

spread.citation: Khandwala et al. 2017 with NVSR 74(1) Table III (2.4); NHSR 179 first-birth gap (2.9).

kinMaleFertilityAgeShiftYears.citation: Years by which a man's children ever born by age lag the women's Census table. NCHS NHSR 179 (NSFG 2015-2019): mean age at first birth 27.0 for men against 24.1 for women (2.9; 2.4 in 2011-2015); life-table medians 27.4 against 24.5. A pure shift understates the gap: men's curve also plateaus lower (72% fathered by 40 against 82% of women).
kinMaleFertilityAgeShiftYears.estimatedFrom: Difference of men's and women's mean age at first birth in NHSR 179 (27.0 minus 24.1).

spread.citation: NHSR 179 mean age at first birth gap, 2011-2015 (2.4) and 2015-2019 (2.9).

kinBirthdayLatestDayOfMonth.citation: Gregorian calendar: the shortest month has 28 days, so any month accepts a generated day from 1 to 28.

personalityHeritability.citation: Vukasovic and Bratko (2015), Heritability of personality: A meta-analysis of behavior genetic studies, Psychological Bulletin 141(4), 769-785: average heritability of personality about 0.40.

personalityUpbringingShift.citation: Standard-score shift per step of the canonical upbringing value added to a resident's temperament; prototype choice so upbringing still matters without overriding the sourced spread.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

personalitySociabilityRiskCorrelation.citation: Costa and McCrae (1992), Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory Professional Manual, facet intercorrelations in the normative sample of 1,000 adults, as transcribed with permission in the psychTools R package dataset neo (version 2.6.4): E2 Gregariousness with E5 Excitement-Seeking, r = .34. Carried as sourced from the NEO-PI-R manual (Costa and McCrae 1992, n = 1,000, via the psychTools dataset); not re-verified against the manual on October 12, 2026. Kept at 0.34, 95% interval 0.284 to 0.394.
personalitySociabilityRiskCorrelation.estimatedFrom: The published facet correlation, applied to the latent temperament scores that the matching facets set (SG-P15-personality-mapping). The spread is the 95% interval for a correlation in a sample of 1,000 (Fisher transformation).

spread.citation: Fisher-transformed 95% interval for the Costa and McCrae (1992) value with N = 1,000.

personalityReliabilityImpulseCorrelation.citation: Costa and McCrae (1992), Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI-R) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory Professional Manual, facet intercorrelations in the normative sample of 1,000 adults, as transcribed with permission in the psychTools R package dataset neo (version 2.6.4): C3 Dutifulness with C6 Deliberation, r = .45; deliberation is reversed to impulsiveness here, so the value is -.45. Carried as sourced from the NEO-PI-R manual (Costa and McCrae 1992, n = 1,000, via the psychTools dataset); not re-verified against the manual on October 12, 2026. Kept at -0.45, 95% interval -0.498 to -0.399.
personalityReliabilityImpulseCorrelation.estimatedFrom: The published facet correlation, applied to the latent temperament scores that the matching facets set (SG-P15-personality-mapping). The spread is the 95% interval for a correlation in a sample of 1,000 (Fisher transformation).

spread.citation: Fisher-transformed 95% interval for the Costa and McCrae (1992) value with N = 1,000.

personalityReferenceAge.citation: Age whose facet curve value counts as average, so the age shifts center near the adult population; prototype choice.

spread.reason: No empirical bound for this generation coefficient has been identified; it is checked through the kin and personality answer keys in the P15 receipt.

spouseAgeGapOpenRowYears.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, CPS 2023 ASEC, America's Families and Living Arrangements: 2023, Table FG3: the age-difference rows are 2-3, 4-5, 6-9, 10-14 and 15-19 years, and the last rows are open (husband or wife 20 or more years older).
spouseAgeGapOpenRowYears.estimatedFrom: Each open row is spread over five whole years, the width of the two rows next to it (10-14 and 15-19 years), so 20 or more years reads as 20 to 24. The open rows hold 1.2% of married couples.

openingCoworkerGroupSize.citation: Typical generated workgroup of residents at one employer (groups are drawn person by person, so sizes vary around it) whose members know each other by name; prototype choice pending a US source on how many coworkers people know. A survey of 3,000 full-time US workers (Olivet Nazarene University, 2019) found five friends at work on average, a lower bound on coworkers known by name. GAME ASSUMPTION. Research found no measured curve of coworkers known by name by workplace size (the repository's P0-6 research says the same); about five friends at work is a lower bound and no upper bound exists.

spread.reason: No US source on the number of coworkers known by name was found; friends at work (about five on average) bound it from below.

griefResilientShare.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months, 94 (45.9%) showed the resilient pattern.
griefResilientShare.estimatedFrom: Taken as the share whose grief has fallen to little by 6 months after a death. The study measured widowed adults aged about 72; the game applies it to every relative's loss (owner ruling, October 10, 2026).

griefChronicShare.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months, 32 (15.6%) showed chronic grief.
griefChronicShare.estimatedFrom: Taken as the share whose grief is still above little at 18 months. The 7.8% with chronic depression began depressed before the loss and are not counted here.

griefEarlyCheckMonths.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months: the first follow-up, 6 months after the loss.

griefLateCheckMonths.citation: Bonanno, Wortman, Lehman et al. (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 83(5):1150-1164, Results: of 205 widowed adults followed at 6 and 18 months: the second follow-up, 18 months after the loss.

griefLittleFraction.citation: Share of the grief at a death that counts as little grief when the resilience spread is solved from Bonanno et al. (2002); the study classified people by depression and grief scores, not by a share of starting grief, so this is a modeling choice.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified; Bonanno et al. (2002) classify grief patterns by scores, not by this quantity.

griefPullWeight.citation: Pull of grief toward rest and contact with family, per unit of grief; no direct source.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified; Bonanno et al. (2002) classify grief patterns by scores, not by this quantity.

griefHoldWeight.citation: Hold of grief on organizing, per unit of grief (negative: grief makes organizing less attractive); no direct source. CTO REVIEW 11: grief first pulls toward withdrawal and family.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified; Bonanno et al. (2002) classify grief patterns by scores, not by this quantity.

schoolFinalGrade.citation: U.S. public schools end with grade 12 (the existing game school-calendar.ts: grades 9-12 in high school).

fallingOutBaseRatePerYear.citation: YouGov, February 24-27, 2023, 31,380 U.S. adults: 68% have decided to end a friendship and followed through; https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/45676-americans-ended-friendship-breakups-poll
fallingOutBaseRatePerYear.estimatedFrom: Solved so 68% of adults have at least one falling-out among the people they shared a class or workgroup with, pooled over six generated towns (seeds p15-fall-a to -f: Grand Mound, Washington; Monument, Colorado; Heber, Utah; Bay Minette, Alabama; Tice, Florida; Summit, New Jersey; 12,963 adults; 1.34 falling-outs per adult). Each generated peer stands for the missing members of a full class or workgroup, so circles sampled from big places count fully. YouGov counts any friendship over a lifetime, not only classmates and coworkers.

fallingOutConflictWeight.citation: Rise in the yearly falling-out rate per level of each person's conflict trait (log scale); no direct source.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified for how temperament changes the rate of falling out.

fallingOutReliabilityWeight.citation: Fall in the yearly falling-out rate per level of each person's reliability (log scale); no direct source.

spread.reason: No empirical range identified for how temperament changes the rate of falling out.

householdChildAgeYears.citation: BLS American Time Use Survey: household children are those under 18 (ATUS glossary, 'household children'); https://www.bls.gov/tus/glossary.htm

unmodeledLeisureValuePerHour.citation: Score an hour of the leisure the game does not model is worth; an act added to a free block after the activation's pick must score above its hours times this. Calibrated so visits fall on the ATUS 2025 share of people who socialize or communicate on a given day (30.4%, Table 1); no direct source for the value itself. Calibrated on two generated towns of 1,000 residents over 28 days (seeds p15-visit-a and -b: Albertville, Alabama; Kennedale, Texas): 0.4 gave 33.9% and 0.5 gave 28.6% of adult-days with a visit.

spread.reason: Calibrated to one ATUS share; no empirical range for the value of an hour of leisure in these score units.

favorSharedHoursPerYear.citation: Hours of time together a year of sharing a class or workgroup counts for when judging closeness at a later need; Hall (2019) finds about 50 hours make a casual friend and that hours working together count less than socializing; no direct source for a year's worth.

spread.reason: No empirical range for hours of friendship time per shared school or work year.

favorRatePerNeed.citation: Talker Research for Safeway Moving, March 19-25, 2025, 2,000 U.S. adults (opt-in commercial poll): 39% first ask friends for help moving; https://talkerresearch.com/more-than-a-third-secretly-hate-being-asked-to-help-with-moving/
favorRatePerNeed.estimatedFrom: Solved so 39% of residents' recorded moves draw a favor from at least one person they shared a class or workgroup with, each sampled peer standing for the missing members of a full group; pooled over six generated towns (seeds p15-fall-a to -f; 6,613 recorded moves into the county, 0.71 favors per move). Asking friends first is not the same as receiving a favor, and the poll is opt-in.

residentsOutlayShareOfIncome.estimatedFrom: Counted households spend this share of last month's income; the rest stands for taxes and saving until income taxes are collected from the counts. 2019 is used rather than 2020–2021, when stimulus and closures pushed saving far above normal.

spread.citation: BEA NIPA Table 2.1, 2020 (pandemic low) to 2022 (low saving).

residentsIncomeWindowMonths.citation: Households smooth spending over income swings (permanent-income behavior); a quarter evens out four- and five-payday months and monthly owner payouts.

spread.citation: From reacting to each month's income to spending from a year's average.

sellerCapacityUtilization.citation: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.17 Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization: total industry capacity utilization averaged 79.6% over 1972–2023; https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/current/
sellerCapacityUtilization.estimatedFrom: A seller's monthly capacity is its projected sales divided by this rate; spending beyond it buys the same thing outside the town (residents travel to the next town). Industrial utilization stands in for retail and service capacity.

spread.citation: G.17 range over business cycles, 1972–2023.

openingRetirementClaimAnchorYearsBeforeF.citation: Calibrated so the opening's retirees claimed at SSA's average age at entitlement, 63.4–65.0 for claims made 2000–2020 (SSA Annual Statistical Supplement 2021, Table 6.B5.1).

spread.citation: From claiming at full retirement age to the earliest claim.

openingRetirementClaimAnchorYearsBeforeF.checkedAgainst: Measured once over three generated openings (seeds claim-a/b/c, 3,694 retirees): mean claim age 64.08 (SSA 63.4–65.0), 20% at 62 (SSA 2021 about 25%); claiming at 70 (SSA about 8%) is not reached yet.

openingRetirementClaimNeedPullYears.citation: People with little saved claim early: in 2021 about a quarter of new retired workers claimed at 62 (SSA Annual Statistical Supplement 2022, Table 6.B5).

spread.citation: From no effect to claiming at 62 from any full retirement age.

openingRetirementClaimNeedPullYears.checkedAgainst: Measured once over three generated openings (seeds claim-a/b/c, 3,694 retirees): mean claim age 64.08 (SSA 63.4–65.0), 20% at 62 (SSA 2021 about 25%); claiming at 70 (SSA about 8%) is not reached yet.

openingRetirementClaimFullBufferMonths.citation: Months of living costs in cash at which savings no longer push an early claim; Federal Reserve SHED 2020: 64% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash.

spread.citation: From an emergency fund to several years of costs.

preStartFromYear.citation: Owner ruling (relayed by the CTO on PR #3999, October 12, 2026): a new game's history runs at coarse steps from 2000 to the start date (M1-14).

spread.citation: How far back coarse history can reach before its run time outweighs what the player sees; checked against the speed rule.

preStartStepMonths.citation: Owner ruling (relayed by the CTO on PR #3999, October 12, 2026): history before the start runs at coarse steps, monthly or quarterly (M1-14).

spread.citation: The two step sizes the pre-start contract offers (src/core2/pre-start.ts).

openingPupilTeacherRatio.citation: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2022, Table 208.20: public elementary and secondary pupil/teacher ratio, fall 2021, 15.4. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d22/tables/dt22_208.20.asp

openingPublicSchoolShare.citation: NCES Fast Facts, Back-to-school statistics: fall 2021 public school enrollment 49.4 million and private 4.7 million; NCES NHES 2019: about 2.8% of school-age children homeschooled.
openingPublicSchoolShare.estimatedFrom: 49.4 / (49.4 + 4.7 + about 1.6 homeschooled) ≈ 0.87 of school-age children enrolled in public schools; pre-K in the public count is not separated.

spread.citation: State public shares range roughly from 0.80 to 0.92 (NCES Digest Table 205.80, private enrollment by state).

openingSchoolAgeFirst.citation: NCES Digest Table 203.10 and Census school-age population: kindergarten through grade 12 serves ages 5–17.

openingSchoolAgeLast.citation: NCES Digest Table 203.10 and Census school-age population: kindergarten through grade 12 serves ages 5–17.

openingTeacherMinimumAge.citation: A bachelor's degree is required for a public school teaching license in every state (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers, How to Become One).
openingTeacherMinimumAge.estimatedFrom: Typical age at a bachelor's degree; the town generator's teacher role uses the same minimum age.

spread.citation: NCES Digest Table 104.10 age at bachelor's completion.

openingWorkingAgeLast.citation: BLS Current Population Survey, labor force participation by age (annual averages): participation falls from about 65% at ages 55–64 to about 19% at 65 and over.
openingWorkingAgeLast.estimatedFrom: New opening jobs go to adults under 65, where most of the labor force is; the opening's part-time rule already starts at 65 (openingPartTimeOlderWorkerAge).

spread.citation: Social Security earliest claim (62) to the delayed-credit end (70).

openingPrivateTuitionAnnualUsd.citation: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2021, Table 205.50: average tuition at all private elementary and secondary schools, 2011–12, $12,420 in constant 2020–21 dollars. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d21/tables/dt21_205.50.asp

openingPrivateSchoolShare.citation: NCES Fast Facts, Back-to-school statistics: fall 2021, 4.7 million private and 49.4 million public elementary and secondary students; NCES NHES 2019: about 2.8% of school-age children homeschooled.
openingPrivateSchoolShare.estimatedFrom: 4.7 / (49.4 + 4.7 + about 1.6 homeschooled) ≈ 0.085 of school-age children in private schools.

spread.citation: State private shares from NCES Digest Table 205.80 range roughly 4% to 14%.

openingCustomerClubMembershipsAnnualNati.citation: BLS, The Economics Daily, 'The new year and household spending' (2026), https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/the-new-year-and-household-spending.htm: Consumer Expenditure Survey, social, recreation and health club memberships, $272 per consumer unit in 2024 (2021: $212).

traitLeanScale.citation: The trait lean difference between two options that counts as a full-strength pull (1) in a formula decision. Starting value: the largest lean difference across generated adults in a 1,200-person drawn town is about 0.6 to 0.7 (OPUS-TRAITS probe, Oct 12, 2026), so the strongest personalities reach about 1, the range of the hand-picked trait sums it replaces.

spread.citation: Generated-town lean differences between options (OPUS-TRAITS probe, Oct 12, 2026): 99th percentile about 0.5, maximum about 0.7.

truthDefaultPull.citation: How strongly a hearer leans toward believing a claim they cannot check, before traits: truth-default theory (Levine 2014, Journal of Language and Social Psychology 33(4)) finds people judge most statements honest. With traitLeanScale, only hearers whose traits lean hard toward doubt (about the most suspicious tenth) doubt a lie.

spread.citation: Levine 2014: truth judgments run well above half in deception experiments; the spread keeps believers a clear majority.

minimumParentAgeAtBirth.citation: The youngest age at which a household's adult is recorded as a child's parent: the Census Bureau's fertility tables count children ever born from age 15 (U.S. Census Bureau, Table 1. Women's Number of Children Ever Born by Age and Marital Status: June 2018, the source of src/core2/data/opening-kin.json fertilityByAge). A younger adult in the home is a sibling or other relative.

traitDecisionWeight.citation: How much a person's scaled trait lean between two options (about -1 to 1, traitLeanScale) adds to a government or civic decision's score when the site has no trait weight of its own (OPUS-TRAITS, Oct 12, 2026). Half a full-strength pull: traits tilt the choice without overriding the record, party and money reasons the site already weighs.

spread.unit: score per unit of scaled trait lean
spread.citation: Starting range; the site reasons it joins run about -1 to 1 (views, warmth, grievance), so the trait term stays a minority share of the total.

circleDecisionDetailDays.citation: Owner rulings, Oct 11 ('save why reasons only for the player and the people they deal with') and Oct 12 (running memory stays small): how long a circle member's act keeps every option's score before only its chosen reasons remain.

spread.citation: A week (the routine retention window, routineRetentionDays) to a season; checked against the memory guard and the 'why' view.

circleActRetentionMonths.citation: Owner ruling, Oct 12 (running memory stays small: keep current state, each person's key facts and recent detail; summarize or drop old detail): how long a circle member's routine act stays in the log after its reasons are condensed.

spread.citation: A season to a three-year term; checked against the memory check (scripts/core2-guard/memory.mjs) and the journal.

openingTeacherAnnualWageUsd.citation: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025, national median annual wage for the game's teacher occupation (profession:teacher), as the town pay table records it (src/simulation/living-world/town-pay.ts, nationalMedianAnnualWage). Used only where a town has no recorded teacher job to copy.

openingTeacherHoursDaily.citation: A full-time teacher's school day where the town has no recorded teacher to copy; the town generator's recorded teacher roles are the reference.

spread.citation: From a 7-hour to an 8.5-hour school day; checked against the town generator's recorded teacher roles.

citizenShareStatePriorAdults.citation: How many adults' worth of the state's CPS citizen share a place's ACS share is blended with, so a small place's noisy sample (ACS 5-year margins) leans on its state.

spread.citation: From trusting a place of a few hundred adults nearly fully to leaning on the state until a place has thousands of adults.

budgetNewGameLoadSeconds.citation: Owner, M7 work order (docs/packages/M7-early-access.md): a new game loads within two minutes while the loading story plays.

spread.citation: The owner's two-minute ceiling; lower is better.

budgetYearSeconds.citation: Owner rule (AGENTS.md, Speed): a town's game year must run in under two minutes.

spread.citation: The owner's two-minute ceiling; lower is better.

budgetSlowestDaySeconds.citation: M7-01: a day advances without visible waiting; the slowest day of a played year must stay under this.

spread.citation: From an instant-feeling day to the longest a player waits without a progress indicator.

budgetSaveCompressedMegabytes.citation: M7-01 save-size budget: The Political Process's saves are 23 to 28 MB at any game length (owner's saves, BOARD Oct 12); ours must stay nowhere near 1.6 GB.

spread.citation: From The Political Process's size to four times it.

schoolDayHours.citation: NCES Schools and Staffing Survey 2011–12: public schools' average school day was about 6.7 hours.
schoolDayHours.estimatedFrom: The national average length of a public school day, used for every school.

spread.citation: Typical public school days across states and districts.
